items.headline: Curfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France
items.blurb: It comes after the country's interior minister admits that police "lost control" in some cities.
items.text: French authorities have imposed overnight curfews in parts of central Paris and other cities after a weekend of riots and looting across the country. Police in Paris said a curfew would be in force between 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) and 06:00 in Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area. A ban on unauthorised gatherings has also been imposed in several other parts of the city centre. Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were announced for cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north. Earlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who has been strongly criticised by opposition politicians over the preparedness for the disorder but whose resignation was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron, admitted police had "lost control" in some cities. items.headline: Beyond money: Why young Tunisians are considering emigration
items.blurb: For many young Tunisians, the question is no longer simply how to make a living, but where they can build a future.
items.text: Tunis, Tunisia – For Maher Qassem, the phrase “beyond money” sums up why he is considering leaving his country. After years of working in the media and trying to secure a stable life for his family, he is now thinking of starting over abroad. Buying a home and planning for a better future have given way to more immediate concerns: covering monthly expenses and meeting mounting financial commitments. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Qassem says almost his entire salary goes towards loan repayments, rent and his son’s education. At times, he adds, he has been unable to help his sick mother pay for medication and treatment. Qassem is among many young Tunisians who see little meaningful change in their daily lives. Seven years into President Kais Saied’s rule, he worries about his son’s prospects and the quality of life the country can offer future generations. Tunisians remain divided between those who believe the past several years have failed to deliver the change they hoped for and those who still believe reform is possible. items.headline: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan
items.blurb: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in…
items.text: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday. Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status. The DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect. items.headline: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
items.blurb: Serhii Beskrestnov says there has not been enough time to warn people about incoming missile attacks. The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing.
items.text: Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People have already died." The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing. The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week , as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows. Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence. On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter." items.text: Saudi Arabia’s Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference has been postponed until next year, according to a statement on the official website, as deadly strikes by the Iran-backed Houthis against the kingdom continue. The annual event was due to start next week on October 26 and run through October 29, with a date next year to be announced “very soon”, the statement released on Tuesday said. FII Institute chief executive officer Dr Maha Bint Mishari Al Saud said the decision “comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates”. “Because this is our landmark tenth edition, we want to ensure it delivers the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect and truly deserves,” she said. Informally dubbed “Davos in the Desert”, a nod to the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Switzerland, the state-backed conference showcases the kingdom’s ambitious investment plans in a bid to attract billions of dollars needed to fund its economic transformation away from hydrocarbons towards tourism, sport and technology. items.text: Paul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutors A Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of ⁠190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history. Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast ⁠in south-eastern Kenya. Prosecutors say Mackenzie and ⁠his Good News International Church organised ​a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended. Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the ⁠court rejected that argument. In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. items.headline: Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
items.blurb: Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie was found guilty of 191 murder charges - all but one of them children.
items.text: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children. Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus". His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil". Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die. Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece". One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows". Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said. items.blurb: Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.
items.text: Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home. Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”. Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries. The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.” Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”. items.headline: Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation
items.blurb: The two top tennis pros married in 2021 and have one child together.
items.text: Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player Gaël Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country. The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside". "This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage. She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget". "Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote. It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said. "Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said. items.blurb: A 27.2 kg mephedrone seizure led EAGLE Force to a clandestine laboratory in Maharashtra, exposing a network of chemical suppliers, equipment dealers and suspected drug manufacturers with links to Hyderabad
items.text: Inside the poultry farm at Maregaon village in Maharashtra’s Gondia district on October 17, the officials found chemical-processing apparatus and remnants of chemicals at the premises. Photo: Special Arrangement A poultry farm in Maharashtra, laboratory equipment purchased in Hyderabad, cash payments exchanged near JNTU in Kukatpally and conversations conducted through encrypted messaging applications were among the clues that helped Telangana’s EAGLE Force uncover an interstate synthetic drug manufacturing network. The investigation, which began with the seizure of 27.2 kg of mephedrone in August, led to the discovery of a suspected clandestine drug manufacturing facility at Maregaon village in Maharashtra’s Gondia district on October 17. Police have identified 24 accused in the wider network, of whom 11 are listed as arrested or in custody, while 13 remain absconding. According to a police complaint dated October 18, the trail of laboratory equipment purchases dates back to March 2024, when a man identifying himself as Krishna approached TVR Scientific Glass Works, a laboratory equipment supplier in Bahadurpally, Hyderabad. items.text: A two-year-old boy died in a suspected case of malnutrition in the Alappuzha district of Keralam, officials said on Monday, with the Kerala State Commission for Protection of Child Rights registering a case. The Child Welfare Committee has meanwhile taken the couple’s four children under its care amid allegations of parental neglect. The deceased, Rahul, was the sixth child of Rajesh, an autorickshaw driver, and Thara, a homemaker who resided in a crumbling rental house in Karthikappally. The two-year-old, found unresponsive by his father early Sunday at their home, was declared dead at a government hospital in Haripad. Another child of the couple had also died a few years ago, officials said, though no clear reasons were attributed to that death. A senior inspector in Thrikkunnapuzha police station, where a case for unnatural death was registered, said a postmortem examination was conducted in Alappuzha following suspicions of negligence. “The autopsy report stated that the child was severely anaemic. items.headline: Allahabad High Court stays conviction of murder convict who wishes to contest 2027 U.P. polls
items.blurb: The court granted bail to the appellant, noting that he was a political figure and an active Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) worker before his conviction
items.text: The Allahabad High Court has stayed the conviction and sentence of a man convicted in a 2017 murder case after noting that he wished to contest the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly election either as an independent candidate or, if possible, on a BJP ticket. A two-judge bench comprising Justice Siddharth and Justice Vinai Kumar Dwivedi passed the order hearing a criminal appeal filed by Nandlal Rai alias Babloo Rai, who was convicted by the Varanasi sessions court in 2025 in connection with a 2017 murder case which was registered at Sigra police station. The court granted bail to the appellant, noting that he was a political figure and an active Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) worker before his conviction. "Keeping in view the right to livelihood of a common man which is not less important than the right to contest election by a politician, conviction and sentence of appellant deserves to be stayed so that he may be able to survive for hearing the final verdict in his above noted appeal," the court added. items.headline: Court cites ‘habitualness’, ‘no respect for law’ in order extending CJP leaders' custody in Jantar Mantar trespassing case
items.blurb: CJP termed the ‘preventive detention’ as ‘a complete mockery of legal process and said it will challenge the order before higher courts ‘immediately.’
items.text: A Special Executive Magistrate court said on Monday that Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das showed “no respect for law” as it extended their judicial custody by two days over the Jantar Mantar protest against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Citing the police investigation, the court order said the CJP leaders had “mobilized and enticed the general public” to gather and hold a protest at Jantar Mantar , which is no longer a designated protest site . The court on Monday rejected their sureties over allegations that they breached security and entered the site during the protest. “The IO further states that both the respondents are members of CJP and they mobilized and enticed the general public to assemble and stage protest at Jantar Mantar, which has been de-notified as a designated protest site,” the court order said, referring to the findings by Investigating Officer (IO). It further added that Ranka and Das, who are lodged in Tihar Jail, flouted their own undertaking of October 11, indicating ‘the apprehension to commit further offence’.

items.text: A British woman tourist was allegedly sexually harassed and had her dress torn by a man while returning to her room in Kerala’s Varkala around 1.30 am on Monday, police said. The accused, identified as Shahad, a resident of Odayam in Varkala, allegedly approached the woman as she was returning to her room after going out for food, and misbehaved with her before tearing her dress, police said, news agency PTI reported. The woman took refuge with a group of tourists, who intervened and stopped the accused. She approached the police on Monday morning, following which a case was registered. Police identified and arrested Shahad with the help of a video recorded by the woman. The accused is expected to be produced before a court on Tuesday for remand. Further investigation is underway, police said. items.headline: How the Polycab case exposes the misuse of IBC for small dues
items.blurb: Insolvency proceedings over minor vendor claims can exert commercial pressure on financially sound companies, even as courts warn against using the bankruptcy code as a debt-recovery tool.
items.text: Bankruptcy proceedings initiated by vendors and suppliers over unpaid dues from large companies are in focus after the insolvency court admitted a plea against wire and cable maker Polycab India on 7 October over an alleged operational debt of ₹ 2.79 crore claimed by supplier Asier Metals. The admission raised concerns among bankruptcy lawyers, given Polycab’s strong financial position, with a net cash balance of ₹ 4,194 crore and shareholders’ net worth of ₹ 12,009 crore in FY26. On 9 October, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) stayed the admission order passed against Polycab by the Ahmedabad bench of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). Insolvency experts said such cases highlight how proceedings can exert commercial pressure on companies even when the amount claimed is relatively small compared with their financial position. “The case highlights an important concern in the existing IBC (Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code) framework. Even a financially sound company may find itself facing insolvency proceedings over a relatively small operational debt,” said Pooja Chakrabarti, partner at Argus Partners. items.headline: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
items.blurb: Penalties are seen as too harsh on motorists who are penalised for parking on private land.
items.text: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham. The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised. In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby . The charge was eventually dropped . Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies". Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat. items.blurb: 23ANDME-BANKRUPTCY/SETTLEMENT (PIX):California settles 23andMe data breach claims for $6 million
items.text: Oct 19 (Reuters) - California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday announced the state will receive a $6 million settlement payment in 23andMe's bankruptcy, resolving California's legal claims related to a 2023 data breach that exposed 6.9 million customers' genetic and other personal information. California had unsuccessfully tried to block the $305 million sale of 23andMe assets to TTAM Research Institute, a nonprofit controlled by 23andMe co-founder Anne Wojcicki. The state had argued that the bankruptcy sale violated California's Genetic Information Privacy Act, and it had said consumers did not give express consent to the sale. Once a trailblazer in DNA testing kits, 23andMe filed for bankruptcy in March 2025, seeking to sell its business at auction after a decline in demand and legal fallout from the data breach. A US bankruptcy judge ruled against California's objections to the sale, and later ruled that the state could not sue to recover money from the bankrupt company's successor. items.headline: Ronaldo given 30-day suspension and £215 fine by Portuguese FA
items.blurb: Cristiano Ronaldo is given a 30-day suspension by the Portuguese Football Federation after leaving his country's international camp last month.
items.text: Cristiano Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension and fined 255 euros (£215) by the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) after leaving his country's international camp last month. The 41-year-old captain walked out of Portugal's Nations League squad in September after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark on 1 October. Ronaldo said in a lengthy statement he had left because Portugal coach Jorge Jesus twice "broke his word", accusing him of an "absolute breach of trust". The Al-Nassr forward's suspension takes effect from the day of the Denmark match, meaning he has already served 19 days of his ban and will not miss any Portugal matches. Portugal face Denmark in the Nations League again on 14 November before travelling to Wales three days later. The FPF disciplinary committee said it took into account "the remorse shown" by Ronaldo in his statement, as well as his "contributions to soccer and recognition for athletic merit". It added that the forward submitted his CV, including his awards and achievements, as part of his defence.

items.headline: Man City star Guehi says taking the knee has lost impact after opting against anti-racism gesture
items.blurb: ‘I don’t think it’s necessarily a football issue; I think it’s a wider societal issue and football is that beacon of hope to try to get the message out,’ said Marc Guehi
items.text: Manchester City's Marc Guehi during the press conference on October 17, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters Manchester City defender Marc Guehi believes the gesture of footballers taking the knee before matches might have lost its impact and wants to see more done in the sport's fight against racism. Guehi, who is Black, didn't take the knee prior to kickoff in City's home game against Ipswich in the Premier League on Saturday (October 17, 2026) in the first of two rounds of games dedicated to the competition's “No Room For Racism” campaign. It isn't the first time Guehi refused to perform the gesture, which was introduced in June 2020 to show support for the Black Lives Matter campaign. Since the start of the 2022–23 season, the Premier League has decided against taking the knee ahead of every match, with players instead invited to do so on certain occasions each season. Speaking Monday (October 19) at a news conference the day before City's Champions League match against AEK Athens, Guehi said it was “great” that the Premier League's anti-racism campaign was continuing.

items.blurb: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people.
items.text: Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots. But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September. The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. items.headline: AI game clones are making indie developers afraid to show their work
items.blurb: Delayed Steam Next Fest demo is a sign of a growing problem for indie devs.
items.text: Since its earliest days, the video game industry has been built on developers creating clones of competing games , with varying levels of originality and varying levels of enforcement from game platforms . Now, though, AI coding tools are making that cloning process so efficient that many developers are getting extremely cautious about sharing their early work too widely. Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend, delaying the launch of a planned public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflux , which had been set to go live with today’s launch of Steam Next Fest . In a post on social media Friday evening , the Alliance Arts team wrote that, in addition to concerns about managing streaming restrictions, “we’re concerned that the demo’s content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game’s presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools and that such works could be released before our launch.” Instead, the developer now plans to share the demo only in “closed sessions” with those who agree to rules regarding posting

items.text: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log. items.text: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry , court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand —potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology , and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations. In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders. The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing. items.blurb: AI companion app Tolan has raised another $30 million after attracting more than 250,000 active users.

Tolan , the AI companion designed to help people manage their daily lives, navigate relationships and emotions, and accomplish their goals, has just expanded its runway with another $30 million in capital. The startup’s investors in the latest round include Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling the total amount it has raised to date and pushing its valuation beyond the previous $120 million, according to a new report by Upstarts Media . (The startup didn’t disclose its new valuation, but PitchBook estimates it at more than $268 million, with “medium confidence.”) Users engage with Tolan’s app through a cartoonish character that’s meant to offer support and help them get through their to-dos. Tolan generates revenue from its tiered memberships, which are required for full access to all features. items.text: Bengaluru-based conversational AI startup Hunar.AI today announced the raise of ₹40 Cr ($4.2 Mn) in its Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures Hunar.AI automates frontline workforce management via its conversational AI agents, which ease various frontline workforce management issues The startup intends to use the fresh capital to strengthen its AI infrastructure, develop its products and bolster its go-to-market strategy Hiring thousands of frontline workers (employees who directly provide goods and services to communities) across multiple cities is a coordination-heavy cumbersome task for HR managers. Recruiters have to call prospective employees, follow up on applications, schedule interviews and keep workers informed through onboarding and training. When hiring volumes spike during festive seasons or business expansion, these tasks can quickly become more difficult to solve manually. Bengaluru-based conversational AI startup Hunar .AI is building AI agents to automate these HR workflows. The startup today announced the raise of ₹40 Cr ($4.2 Mn) in its Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures. items.headline: Mobavenue’s Tejas Rathod On The Shift From Ad Optimisation To AI Decisioning
items.blurb: A high click rate cannot tell a fintech company whether a user will complete the KYC. Similarly, downloading an app…
items.text: As digital advertising shifts from clicks and installs towards measurable business outcomes, AI is increasingly being used to predict user intent and optimise decisions beyond the immediate media event In a conversation with Inc42, Mobavenue’s founder and CTO Tejas Rathod explains how the company is building AI-driven advertising infrastructure around real-time decisioning, privacy-conscious signals and continuous learning From processing more than 1.25 Bn data signals a day to connecting awareness, acquisition and activation, Rathod discusses how he sees intelligence evolving across the digital marketing lifecycle A high click rate cannot tell a fintech company whether a user will complete the KYC. Similarly, downloading an app does not promise a purchase. Yet these remain the metrics that digital advertising has traditionally been built around. For brands, the real challenge is understanding whether a click or app download will actually translate into a business outcome. As advertisers demand clearer links between media spending and business outcomes, adtech is moving towards systems that can predict intent, learn from downstream behaviour and optimise for what happens beyond the click or install.
